summary: This RFC defines algorithm names and parameters for using some SHA-2 hash algorithms for data integrity verification in SSH. It updates RFC 4253 by adding a new recommended integrity algorithm.

eli5.summary: SSH puts a fingerprint on each message so changes are noticed. This adds stronger fingerprint recipes.

questions: does ssh support sha-2 for mac
which hmac algorithms does ssh use
subtitle: Adds two SHA-2 based HMAC algorithms for checking that SSH messages were not altered.

tldr.problem: SSH defined data integrity checks only with SHA-1 and MD5, and security concerns about both led implementors and users to ask for SHA-2 options.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines two new MAC algorithm names, hmac-sha2-256 (RECOMMENDED) and hmac-sha2-512 (OPTIONAL), in the style of RFC 4253.
tldr.outcome: RFC 4253 is updated with a new RECOMMENDED integrity algorithm, and both names were registered with IANA.

today: RFC 6668 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 4253. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why SHA-2 for SSH
sections.content:
The Secure Shell (SSH) is described as a very common protocol for secure remote login. At the time, it defined data integrity verification using the SHA-1 and MD5 algorithms, as specified in RFC 4253.

Because of security concerns about both algorithms (see RFC 6194 and RFC 6151), implementors and users asked for integrity verification with members of the SHA-2 family. This memo updates RFC 4253 by specifying a new RECOMMENDED data integrity algorithm.
sections.eli5: The two old fingerprint recipes were starting to worry people. So people asked for newer, stronger ones.

sections.title: The New MAC Algorithms
sections.content:
Two data integrity algorithms are defined, using the naming style and conventions of RFC 4253. hmac-sha2-256 is RECOMMENDED and uses a 32-byte digest and a 32-byte key. hmac-sha2-512 is OPTIONAL and uses a 64-byte digest and a 64-byte key.

The HMAC mechanism comes from RFC 2104 and was updated in RFC 6151, and the SHA-2 family is defined in FIPS 180-3. HMAC-SHA2-224 and HMAC-SHA2-384 were considered but left out, because they have the same computational requirements as the 256 and 512 variants and do not seem to be much used in practice.

Users, implementors and administrators may put the new MACs into their proposal ahead of the REQUIRED hmac-sha1 algorithm from RFC 4253, so that they are negotiated first. Test vectors for HMAC with SHA-2 are in RFC 4231.
sections.eli5: There are two new recipes: a medium one that is recommended and a bigger one that is optional. If you prefer, you can ask to try them before the old standby.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content: IANA updated the Secure Shell (SSH) Protocol Parameters registry. The MAC Algorithm Names hmac-sha2-256 and hmac-sha2-512 were added, both pointing to Section 2 of this RFC. This augments the MAC algorithm names in RFC 4253 and RFC 4250.
sections.eli5: The new recipe names were written in the official list so everyone spells them the same way.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations of RFC 4253 apply. The RFC also cites NIST Special Publication 800-107 and NIST SP 800-131A, which suggest that HMAC-SHA1 and HMAC-SHA2-256 have a security strength of 128 bits and 256 bits, respectively, and that these are considered acceptable key lengths.

It adds that many users seem to be interested in the perceived safety of using SHA-2 based algorithms for hashing.
sections.eli5: The old safety rules still apply, and the experts say the new recipe is strong enough.
